title: Cluster Info, Contexts & Namespaces
intro: Before you touch pods, you need to know which cluster and namespace you're even pointed at — that's what causes 'it's not there!' panics more than anything else.

steps.prompt: Check what cluster kubectl is currently talking to.
steps.fake_output:
Kubernetes control plane is running at https://10.0.0.1:6443
CoreDNS is running at https://10.0.0.1:6443/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/services/kube-dns:dns/proxy
steps.explanation: This confirms you actually have a working connection before you waste time debugging 'nothing works'.
steps.why: 'kubectl version' also confirms connectivity but only returns version numbers — cluster-info is the one that actually shows you the control plane and DNS endpoints.

steps.prompt: See which context (cluster+user+namespace combo) you're currently using.
steps.explanation: Multiple clusters (prod, staging, local) usually live in one kubeconfig — this tells you which one is active right now.
steps.why: 'kubectl config get-contexts' lists all of them with a * next to the active one — current-context is faster when you just need the one answer.

steps.prompt: List all namespaces in the cluster.
steps.fake_output:
NAME              STATUS   AGE
default           Active   30d
kube-system       Active   30d
production        Active   12d
steps.explanation: Resources are scoped to a namespace by default — if you don't see something with kubectl get pods, it might just be in a different namespace.
steps.why: 'ns' is the short alias for 'namespaces', same idea as 'po' for pods or 'deploy' for deployments.

steps.prompt: Switch your active namespace to 'production' so you don't have to type -n production on every command.
steps.explanation: This changes the default namespace for the current context — every following command now targets 'production' unless you override it.
steps.why: You could add '-n production' to every single command instead, but that gets old fast and is easy to forget on the one time it matters most.
